UX CASE STUDY / WHISK

Whisk: cooking, made for little hands.

Whisk is a recipe and tutorial website that helps kids cook simple dishes on their own, safely. Each recipe is broken into one step at a time that kids can replay, slow down or control by voice, while parents filter recipes by age, tools and allergies.

Background

Kids want to help in the kitchen, but recipes and cooking videos are made for adults. Parents end up stepping in at the scary parts, and cleanup turns into an argument.

Goals
  • Help kids cook simple dishes on their own, safely
  • Give parents content they trust is age-appropriate
  • Make cleanup and small wins part of the habit
My role
  • Solo UX/UI designer
  • Research, IA, wireframes, UI and skeuomorphic UI assets
Duration & tools
  • Sep 2025 – present
  • Interaction Design Principles, Northeastern
  • Paper, Miro, Figma
PrototypeResearchDefineJourneyIdeateStructureEvolutionScreensReflect

The prototype today One step at a time, in a kitchen made for kids

This is Whisk as it runs in my Figma prototype right now. The screens below aren’t pictures: they are the same live cooking, Play and scrapbook pages that sit inside the prototype, running in your browser.

Figma prototype · Teddy bear pancakes

Laptop the full kitchen · iPad where Natalia actually cooks · Phone the scrapbook, stacked for one hand

Play the Figma prototype ↗The big screen above is interactive. Tap I did it! to cook a step.
For kids

One step per screen. Replay, slow down or say “again” with messy hands.

For parents

Filter by age, tools and allergies. Risky steps flag when a grown-up should help.

For both

Tidy-up checkpoints between steps, and a “done!” moment that saves the dish to the scrapbook.

01 Understanding the problem Interviews with nine parent-child pairs

I interviewed nine parent-child pairs about safety, motivation and how kids actually cook at home. My deepest conversation was with Liz and her 9-year-old daughter Natalia, using a 30 to 60 minute script that moved from warm-up questions to motivations, a recent cooking session, barriers, and a “magic wand” question.

TikTokis where Liz finds recipes, but adult videos move too fast for kids
iPadis Natalia’s device, at least 2 hours of screen time a day, including schoolwork
Hot oiland seasoning were the only steps where Natalia needed her mom’s guidance
Cleanupled to arguments over messes and putting tools away

One time she cooked noodles for me when I was sick. Her independence moved me.

Liz, on a moment that felt successful

I wish there were a magic wand to take away the feeling of making things wrong.

Liz, on the magic wand question

Paraphrased from my interview notes.

Affinity map

I sorted my notes into five groups, then tagged each note by how much it affected a kid’s safety and independence: Must-have Nice-to-have Risk

Pain points
Afraid of hot oil splashingAdult recipes are long and confusingArguments over cleanupDoesn’t know which seasoning to use
Needs
Simple, age-appropriate menusReplay, rewind and slow downWarnings for chili, garlic and allergiesVoice control with messy handsNutrition info per meal
Ideas from Liz
Several ways to season the same dishRecipes for a parent and child togetherAn open discussion section
Constraints
Kid-sized knives, no sharp-edged toolsUsed on an iPad in the kitchenKids sharing photos online
Insights
Less picky about food she makes herselfMaking food for family is the proudest momentWants to play with ingredients, like drawing on frosty tomatoes

02 Problem statement How might we help kids cook on their own, safely, and feel proud of it?

I defined the problem around the three most critical pain points from the research.

1Scary steps

Hot oil and sharp tools make kids stop, and parents take over.

2Recipes built for adults

Long, fast videos and text that kids can’t follow at their own pace.

3Messy endings

Cleanup becomes a fight, and mistakes feel like failing.

Personas

Whisk serves two people at once, so I made a primary persona for the child and a secondary persona for the parent.

N
Natalia, 93rd grade, inquisitive, imaginative, sometimes hesitant
Goals

Cook simple dishes on her own, experiment with ingredients, and make food her family is proud of.

Pain points

Afraid of hot oil and sharp tools. Gets discouraged when things go wrong or messy. Adult recipes are confusing and too long.

L
Liz Harper, 52Accountant, mom of Natalia, responsible, patient, practical
Needs

Step-by-step, voice-guided recipes for kids, cleanup tips, and a space to celebrate her child’s progress.

Pain points

Safety worries, messy cleanup, and hard-to-find age-appropriate content.

03 User journey Natalia makes scrambled eggs

I mapped the last dish Natalia made, step by step from the interview. In the As-Is journey her mood drops at hot oil and at cleanup. The To-Be journey shows where Whisk lifts each low point.

As-Is, todayTo-Be, with Whisk
Pick a recipeTikTok videos made for adultsFilters for age, tools and allergies
Hot oilScared of splashes, mom guides the stepRisk meter warns early, “ask a grown-up”
SeasonUnsure what goes with whatA few ways to finish the same dish
Clean upLeft to the end, then an argumentSmall tidy-up checkpoints between steps

04 Ideation From ideas to a focused feature set

I benchmarked three recipe sites in Chrome DevTools, sketched ideas against each pain point, and ranked them with the MoSCoW method so the first version stays small and safe.

Vincenzo’s Plate ↗

WorksClear collapsed menu and a well-placed recipe button with strong contrast.

BreaksRecipe images aren’t clickable, and the text doesn’t look like a link.

 Barley & Birch ↗

WorksActivities grouped by season, with bright graphics that invite kids to click.

BreaksLink overlays have no accessible name and can’t be reached by keyboard.

 America’s Test Kitchen Kids ↗

WorksFilters make recipes easy to narrow down, and search sits at the top.

BreaksA large sign-up form feels stressful, and the light background hurts readability.
Must have

Step-by-step tutorials with replay and 0.75× speed

Filters for age, tools and allergies

Risk meter with “ask a grown-up” alerts

Should have

Voice control: “again”, “next”, “slower”

Tidy-up checkpoints between steps

Several ways to season one dish

Could have

Cook-together recipes with a calendar

Community gallery of creations

Nutrition info for each meal

Won’t have, yet

An open discussion forum, until there’s moderation built for kids

05 Information architecture Three primary workflows

1

Find a recipe. Search, add filters for age, tools and allergies, then pick from the results.

2

Cook along. Follow the tutorial one step at a time, replaying or slowing down any step, with safety alerts.

3

Share a creation. Celebrate the finished dish, then choose to share it or keep it private.

06 Iteration How Whisk evolved

Whisk went from paper, to a first clickable prototype I tested with users, to a second version, to the live cooking screens it has today. Here is what changed at each step, and why.

PaperV1 · Nov 3V2Now

Paper Thinking it through by hand

Before any screen, I worked out the rules on paper: what Whisk should stand for, who decides what, and how a kid moves from picking a dish to sharing it.

Early paper wireframes for the homescreen, cooking along and sharing.

V1 · Nov 3 The first clickable prototype

V1 put the paper ideas into Figma: the homescreen as a kitchen wall with tools hanging on a rail, dishes under cake domes, and the first cooking screens. I froze it on its own page and put it in front of users.

“The text is really thin, I had to squint. Some of the pictures aren’t clear, I wasn’t sure what I was supposed to do. And the hand looks like a chicken cutlet! When I finished cooking there was no way back, I was just stuck on the last step.”

Feedback from a tester on V1, paraphrased
Thin, hard-to-read textGraphics that didn’t explain the stepA hand that looked like a chicken cutletNo way back after cookingButtons that went nowhereCooking screens squeezed under two header bars

V2 Nothing is a dead end

V2 kept V1 untouched for comparison and fixed the navigation first, so testers could always get somewhere.

  • Every button goes somewhere. The Saved star opens Saved recipes, and the menu icon opens a real menu with 11 places to go.
  • New pages for Saved recipes, Previous creations, Discover recipes and About Whisk, each with a working Back button.
  • Things you tap now change. Time chips and category tiles switch the Create drawer, on the website, iPad and iPhone layouts. Allergy, knife, heat and plug-in chips select when tapped.
  • A friendly “We’re still cooking this page!” screen, with Jelly waving, Go back and Back to the kitchen, for anything not built yet.
  • A clear test path. Old explorations moved to an archive, and a “Start here” screen lists the tester tasks.

Now Live cooking screens

The cooking screens are now live pages inside the prototype. Each piece of V1 feedback has a fix you can see:

Feedback“The text is thin”

Steps and buttons now use bigger type, and every step is one short sentence with a plain helper line underneath.

Feedback“The pictures aren’t clear”

Each step has its own picture of the action. The tools for that step light up on the counter, and the safety meter says it in words: All good, Careful hands or Hot!

Feedback“The hand looks like a chicken cutlet”

I redrew the hand so it reads clearly as a hand doing the action, in every step that shows one.

Feedback“There’s no way back”

The last step ends on a “done!” screen that saves the dish to the scrapbook, with Cook again and Back to the kitchen.

Found in testingSqueezed screens

The cooking page now uses one header, with Chef age moved into the title row, so everything fits the Figma screen with nothing cut off.

Found in testingDead ends

Recipes that aren’t built yet land on the “still cooking” screen instead of nowhere.

07 Final solution Screens for every purpose

Every screen below is the live prototype, set to a different moment. Each one answers a need from the research.

Six recipes live in the prototype

Plus Teddy bear pancakes and Bunny-shaped apples above. Six recipes cook live in the Figma prototype.

08 Reflection & next steps What I learned

Primary users change the design

I didn’t expect interviews to drive functional decisions like filters, replay controls and cleanup prompts. They also made me a better interviewer: I learned to capture highlights quickly and distill them.

Design is about how people feel

Natalia’s joy in simple tasks and her fear of burns showed me that good design helps people feel proud of themselves and supported, not just that it looks good.

Designing for two users at once

Every feature had to work for a child and reassure a parent. The risk meter does both: it slows the kid down and tells the parent when to step in.

Next round of testing

Task 1

Find a no-knife recipe for a 9-year-old

Task 2

Replay a step and finish it without help

Task 3

Finish a recipe and choose to share or keep it

What I’ll measure

Tasks completed without a parent stepping in, time on each step, and how confident parents feel letting their child cook

The idea is already growing beyond the screen: in Northeastern’s XR lab I’m prototyping a passthrough cooking interface on Quest 3 that guides kids through recipes hands-free.

CAMPAIGN CASE STUDY / NINJA PREPI

The only cheating we encourage.

Ninja’s PREPi slices, shreds, crinkles and chops in one compact bowl. Our brief was to make it a must-have for college students. I helped build the creative platform, three creator-led TikTok concepts and the key visual, and planned how we’d launch and measure it.

Unlaunched campaign concept, class project
Type
Creative campaign concept
Audience
College students in dorms
Channel
TikTok creator content
Deliverables
Platform, 3 concepts, key visual
Audience insightCreative strategyCopywritingArt directionStoryboardingCreator strategyCampaign planning
InsightStrategyConceptsDevelopmentPressure testLaunch

The brief

Make a kitchen tool feel like a dorm must-have.

College students already know fresh food is better. They don’t make it because a dorm has no counter, no room to cut anything, and their days run from class to practice to everything else. So the default is the dining hall or overpriced takeout. The campaign had to make PREPi the shortcut, not another chore.

01 Insight Three reasons students don’t cook

Every reason students gave up on fresh food came back to one of three tensions. Each one became a job for the campaign.

Space
No surface to cut food on in a dormThe dorm is too small to do everything the hard way
Time
No time for the dining hall between class and practiceLunch happens in the gap between classes
Effort & cost
Takeout is the easy option, and it’s overpricedWants something actually fresh, with minimal effort
Space

Students have no space for cutting food in their dorms.

Time

Students don’t always have time for the dining hall or eating out when balancing class and extracurriculars.

Effort

It has to work anywhere, with minimal effort, or it won’t get used.

02 Strategy Who we’re talking to

The audience

A busy college student in a dorm who wants fresh, good-looking food but has no kitchen and a packed schedule. They find products through creators on TikTok, and their room has a look. Our moodboard leaned into that world: strawberry matcha, soft pinks and greens.

The shift

Students hear “don’t cheat” all through college. We flipped it: cooking the hard way is optional, and cheating the prep is smart.

  • How might we make fresh prep possible with no counter at all?
  • How might we fit cooking into the gaps between class and practice?
  • How might we make a kitchen tool feel like a dorm must-have, not a chore?

03 Concepts From platform to creator ideas

“The only cheating we encourage.”

We believe in college kids cheating.

Cheating on the dining hall. Cheating on the overpriced takeout meal. Cheating your way to something actually fresh.

College gets too busy, and your dorm is probably too small to do everything the hard way. So cheat the prep, and keep the credit.

Each concept answers one insight, so together they cover every reason students give up.

Answers: Space

POV: Shredded cucumber

Creators known for recent heartbreaks channel their frustration into chopping a cucumber with PREPi in a tiny dorm-like room.

Hooks “If my man ever cheats on me…” / “POV: a man interrupts me”

@alixearle, @tiannarobillard

Answers: Effort

So easy you can do it in your Twin XL

Creators make fresh crinkle fries on a dangerously clean white dorm bed. No kitchen, no counter. Confidence, then chaos, then craving.

Hooks “My RA cannot see this” / “Who said you need a kitchen?”

@lazypotnoodle

Answers: Time

Day in the life

A student-athlete creator uses PREPi from morning practice to a friend’s birthday, showing it as a new dorm must-have.

Hooks “Girl math is cheating on the dining hall” / “Girl dinner made right in the dorm”

@abbipriv, @livviazhang

Visual direction

StrawberryBerryMatchaLeafForest

04 Creative development Finding the key visual

Three layout directions, each weighting the headline, product and attitude differently, before landing on the final poster.

Pink “cheating”

The one word that carries the joke gets the strawberry color, so it lands first.

Forest green type

Pulled from the matcha side of the moodboard. It reads clearly on pink without feeling harsh.

Five icons

Slice, shred, crinkle, chop and prep sit at the bottom as proof, without crowding the hero.

“Work smarter. Eat fresher.”

A plain-spoken support line that turns the joke into a reason to buy.

Twin XL video, frame by frame

The video follows the beat from our concept: confidence, then chaos, then craving.

05 Pressure test What could go wrong

Before pitching, I looked at where each concept could fall flat, and how we’d protect it.

ConceptWhy it worksRiskHow we’d handle it
Shredded cucumberThe strongest hook. Breakup humor is built to be shared.Jokes about cheating can feel mean, or off-brand for Ninja.Keep the joke on the cucumber, never a real person, and have creators approve the script.
Twin XLThe clearest proof that you don’t need a kitchen.Cooking on a bed can look fake, or break dorm rules.Make the rule-breaking the joke (“My RA cannot see this”) and end on clean sheets.
Day in the lifeThe most realistic, and shows PREPi used three times a day.A crowded format that’s easy to scroll past.Show PREPi in the first second, and lead with the “girl math” hook.

06 Launch & measure If this went live

Rollout around the school year

  1. Move-in weekThe key visual and short teasers, timed to when students are buying dorm essentials.
  2. First month of classesThe three creator videos go live, one concept a week.
  3. MidtermsA “cheat day” follow-up, when students are busiest and most likely to skip the dining hall.

How we’d know it worked

Hook hold

Share of viewers still watching after 3 seconds

Saves & shares

Signals that students want to try it

Dorm comments

Comments mentioning dorms, roommates or RAs

Clicks

Visits to the PREPi page from creator links

First test: post two hooks for the same video and keep the one that holds viewers longer.

03.APP DESIGN · TEAM OF FOUR

SleepyPaws

Sleep on track, for your pet’s sake.

A gamified sleep app where a virtual pet’s mood depends on how well you slept. Hit your sleep goal and you unlock toys, accessories and new worlds. Miss it, and your pet is too tired to play.

Try the Figma prototype ↗
Team
Doris Egbujie, Nicole Shao, La Zhuo Anggilam, Kate Crabtree
My role
UX designer: reward loops, UI, toy and theme art
Timeline
Nov – Dec 2024
Tools
Figma, Procreate
QuestionResearchPlanStyleOnboardingIterateCore loopFinalReflection

01.THE QUESTIONCan caring for a pet fix your sleep?

How might a pet that depends on your sleep motivate you to go to bed on time?

We designed for young adults, 18 to 30, who struggle to keep a sleep schedule: college students juggling class and jobs, early-career professionals working late, and anyone losing sleep to gaming, binge-watching or late-night scrolling.

Meet Alex, 20

After a long day of studying and gaming, Alex keeps waking up exhausted. They want 8 hours a night, and they don’t want to see their virtual cat unhappy.

02.RESEARCHWhat already works

We looked at apps that turn habits into games, like Forest, Habitica, Finch, Pokémon Sleep and the original Tamagotchi, and read three studies on gamification and virtual pets.

Rewards work

Gamification improved health habits most when it included rewards, challenges and social interaction.

Pets create attachment

Digital companions can shape behavior and build emotional engagement.

It transfers

Virtual pets already motivate people to exercise, so the same pull could apply to sleep.

03.SKETCH & PLANFrom doodles to four flows

  1. 1Choose a pet and change the background theme
  2. 2Log sleep, then play when your pet is happy
  3. 3Log sleep when you missed your goal, and your pet is upset
  4. 4Check your sleep data and your pet’s mood for the week

04.STYLE GUIDEA night sky with one warm light

The whole app lives at night: four blues from twilight to midnight, white for anything you read, and a single orange for anything you press. Sampled from our Figma file.

Twilight#4C6FC6
Moonlight#C9D6F7
Midnight#2C48A7
Periwinkle#7B9DED
Button + accent#FF8A0A
Text#FFFFFF
Aa

Headers Inter, Bold, 32

Aa

Text SF Pro Display, Regular, 24

✦✦

Logo a crescent moon resting on two clouds

05.ONBOARDINGSeven screens to a pet of your own

Onboarding collects only what the game needs: who you are, how old you are, when you want to sleep and wake on each day, and which pet will be waiting. The schedule is set per day, so a late Friday doesn’t count against you.

Screens 01–06 rebuilt in code from the Figma file. Screen 07 and every screen below are the original Figma screens.

06.ITERATEThree rounds in Figma

The basics. A home screen with three buttons, a pet page with care icons, a sleep log with a quality rating, and a weekly chart with the percentage of goals met.

The pet reacts. After logging sleep, the cat is either proud of you or disappointed. A new home screen shows today’s hours and the pet’s mood, overall quality became a cat face, and a bottom nav bar was added.

Reasons to come back. Choose a cat, dog or parakeet, set sleep goals for specific days, unlock themes and toys by meeting goals, and wait a week for more.

07.THE CORE LOOPOne night, start to finish

Every day runs through the same loop. The home screen answers one question at a glance, how did I sleep, with a single big number and a pet whose face already says it.

→ → or

Why one number. Today’s hours is the largest thing on the home screen. Everything else, pets, mood, nav, sits around it.

Why the pet speaks. The pet’s line under the stage turns a statistic into a feeling: “She is feeling happy and energetic today!”

Why orange. Orange is the only warm color, so the nav bar and every button read as “press me” against the night.

08.FINALTwo ways the night can go

09.REFLECTIONLooking back, two years and a lot of projects later

SleepyPaws was my first app built with a team, and the first time I designed a reward loop instead of a single screen. Reading the Figma file again now, I can see clearly what held up, and what I’d design differently.

What held up

A loop you can explain in one line

Sleep well, your pet is happy, you unlock things. Every screen in the final flow serves that sentence, which kept four designers pointed the same way.

Emotion before data

Leading with the pet’s mood, and leaving the chart for later, made the app feel like caring for someone rather than being graded.

A tiny, consistent system

Four blues, white and one orange. It made the night theme feel calm, and it made the rewards, the only colorful things, feel special.

What I’d change

a.
Punishment can backfire.

Locking care after a bad night risks making people feel they failed, which is the opposite of what someone short on sleep needs. I’d reward progress instead: a pet that is a little sleepy but still glad to see you, and a small reward for getting closer to the goal than last night.

b.
Honesty is a design problem.

Manual logging makes it easy to type 8 hours and unlock everything. Connecting to Apple Health or Google Fit, with manual entry as a fallback, would make the game fair and remove a whole screen from the daily loop.

c.
Not everyone sleeps at night.

The schedule assumes a nighttime sleeper. Shift workers, new parents and people with sleep disorders were left out. Day-by-day goals were a start; next I’d let the goal be total sleep across 24 hours, including naps.

d.
The orange buttons fail contrast.

White text on our orange measures about 2.4:1, well under the 4.5:1 WCAG asks for. White on the periwinkle tiles is about 2.7:1. Keeping the orange and switching the label to the navy we already had gives about 5.6:1, with no change to the look.

e.
The nav bar needs words.

Four white icons on orange, with no labels and no selected state. A small label under each icon and a clear active tab would make the bar easier to learn on day one.

f.
We tested too little.

We only had limited usability testing. If I did it again, I’d put the onboarding and a single logging night in front of five people after iteration 1, before we built the reward system on top.

What I took with me

Designing the toys and themes taught me that a reward only works if you want it before you have it, so the locked state deserves as much care as the unlocked one. Working as one of four taught me to name decisions out loud, like “one warm color” or “the pet speaks first,” so the whole team can design from the same rules. I’ve carried both into Whisk and into my game work since.

Next ideas: mini-games and seasonal pets tied to streaks, tailored bedtime routines, and smarter reminders when you’re still on your phone late at night.
